query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing lattice distortion in multimetal nanoparticles by substituting one constituent with an element that has a larger atomic radius and higher mixing enthalpy penalty raises the atomic diffusion activation barrier, thereby delaying temperature‐induced phase segregation and chemical ordering across catalytic and thermoelectric operating temperatures (473–1923 K).
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near‐equal atomic ratios, initially crystallized as a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
generation.intervention: Substitute one of the constituents with an element that induces greater lattice distortion (due to a larger atomic radius mismatch and higher mixing enthalpy penalty) while maintaining an overall equimolar composition.
generation.conditions: Testing under controlled catalytic and thermoelectric environments using inert atmospheres with a temperature ramp from 473 K to 1923 K; all synthesis parameters and environmental conditions are kept constant across samples.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice distortion arising from increased atomic size mismatch and unfavorable mixing enthalpy, which elevates the energy barrier for atomic diffusion.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced lattice distortion increases the effective barrier to atomic diffusion, counteracting the temperature-driven drive for elemental segregation and chemical ordering. This competition between entropy-driven homogeneous mixing and thermally activated diffusion determines the structural stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with enhanced lattice distortion are predicted to maintain homogeneous single-phase crystallinity and uniform elemental distribution to higher temperatures compared to baseline nanoparticles. In situ high-temperature XRD should show delayed changes (e.g., peak shifts or emergence of secondary phases), and elemental mapping techniques should reveal reduced segregation.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles with an unmodified composition (minimal lattice distortion) that display earlier onset of phase segregation and chemical ordering when subjected to the same high-temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: This prediction holds when synthesis, atmosphere, and heating procedures are identical, ensuring that the only variable is the degree of lattice distortion. Results may differ if reactive atmospheres or extrinsic kinetic effects are present.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature shift at which phase segregation is delayed and the quantitative increase in diffusion activation energy remain uncertain until experimentally determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA nanoparticles: one with the baseline composition (minimal lattice distortion) and one in which one constituent is replaced by an element that produces greater lattice distortion. Subject both sets to identical catalytic/thermoelectric test conditions by ramping the temperature from 473 K to 1923 K in an inert atmosphere. Conduct in situ high-temperature XRD and elemental mapping (using EDS or atom probe tomography) to monitor phase purity and elemental distribution.
measurements: In situ high-temperature XRD to track peak positions, shifts, and emergence of secondary phases
Elemental mapping to assess spatial chemical homogeneity and detect any segregation
If feasible, kinetic measurements to estimate atomic diffusion coefficients
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles with enhanced lattice distortion do not exhibit a statistically significant delay in the onset of phase segregation or do not maintain a more homogeneous elemental distribution compared to the baseline sample, or if diffusion kinetics remain similar between the two sets, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted much attention in various fields with regard to applications as structural materials, biomaterials, supercapacitors, and catalysts., HEAs comprise mixtures of five or more metallic elements at near equiatomic ratios and form simple single solid-solution phases having lattice structures including face-centered cubic (fcc) and body-centered cubic (bcc)., The high configurational entropy of these alloys stabilizes the solid-solution phase such that this phase appears rather than an intermetallic phase or phase segregation., The severe lattice distortion in these materials that results from differences in the atomic sizes of the constituent elements also causes low atomic diffusivity. The unique synergistic effects resulting from combining multiple elements provide high specific strength, ductility, corrosion resistance, and thermal stability, such that HEAs are unique and fascinating materials. In recent years, many researchers have reported that HEA nanoparticles (NPs) having sizes on the nanometer scale (that is, in the range of 1 to 100 nm) show promise with regard to catalytic applications. This implies that there could be an upper bound on the extent of atomic size dispersion allowable in HEAs. The relevance of this rule to HEAs is an open question deserving further investigation; for example, see Ref. (). We demonstrate that temperature and lattice distortion jointly contribute to numerous thermodynamic, structural, and elastic properties via a unified effective temperature, encompassing both the actual temperature and the extent of lattice distortion. Lattice distortion notably enhances the stability of a single-phase solid solution, as commonly found in binary and multicomponent alloys, by elevating the effective temperature. Increasing temperature further reinforces the stability of a solid solution compared to phase separation or ordering. To ascertain the phase stability of a HEA system, we utilized the Hume–Rothery rules. These foundational principles elucidate the conditions under which a multiprincipal-component metallic system can form a solid solution or other phases. To predict the formation of a single-phase solid solution, two primary criteria have been widely used. The first is the atomic radius difference, quantifying the variation in atomic sizes of the components in a mixture or compound, where ci represents the molar ratio of component i and r is the atomic radius. A higher value of δ indicates a greater disparity in the sizes of the atoms present, which can influence the material’s structural and electronic properties. A smaller δ is preferable to minimize internal stress, which impedes random diffusion and mixing. The dispersion stability of the MEA-NPs can be explained by the following two reasons. First, we used high temperatures for the MEA-NP synthesis, and as a result, they naturally have high thermal stability. Second, the defects of the carbon nanofibers help to anchor these MEA-NPs onto the substrate with improved thermal stability. In terms of the observed structural stability, we believe that it originates from the entropy stabilization effect. Thermodynamically, multi-elemental mixing increases the mixing of entropy and favors an alloy structure. Kinetically, the mixing among different elements also leads to increased lattice distortion (table S3 for Ru MEA-NPs) and, therefore, sluggish diffusion, which prevents phase separation and elemental segregation (, ). frame.system: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near‐equal atomic ratios, initially crystallized as a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
frame.goal: Determine the mechanistic factors that enable or impede the maintenance of structural and chemical stability across catalytic and thermoelectric operating temperatures (473–1923 K).
frame.limitation: It is not well understood what drives or suppresses phase segregation, chemical ordering, or lattice reconstruction under high-temperature catalytic/thermoelectric conditions even when starting from a homogeneous solid solution.
root_cause_cues: initially crystallized as a solid solution
constraints: Equal or near-equal atomic ratios of at least five metals
Operating conditions spanning 473–1923 K under catalytic and thermoelectric environments
frame.regime: Catalytic and thermoelectric conditions with a temperature range from 473 K to 1923 K, where high temperature may activate diffusion and segregation processes.
prior_attempts: Previous studies have largely assumed that high configurational entropy ensures stability without adequately accounting for temperature-activated atomic diffusion and local lattice distortions.
Attempts focusing solely on thermodynamic descriptors (like mixing entropy or average enthalpy) have fallen short in predicting stability under realistic catalytic conditions.
frame.mechanistic_hypothesis: The hypothesis is that the competition between high configurational entropy (which favors a single-phase solid solution) and temperature-induced atomic diffusion (which promotes elemental segregation and local lattice rearrangements) governs stability. Specifically, when temperature-driven diffusion overcomes the stabilization provided by lattice distortions (due to atomic size mismatch) and favorable mixing enthalpy, the nanoparticles will exhibit phase separation or chemical ordering. A controlled comparison would involve synthesizing nearly identical nanoparticles but systematically varying an element known to affect lattice distortion (or mixing enthalpy) while keeping overall atomic ratios constant.
frame.controlled_comparison: Prepare two sets of nanoparticles: one with a stronger lattice distortion characteristic (via inclusion of an element with a larger size mismatch and higher mixing enthalpy penalties) and one with minimal distortion. Evaluate both sets under identical catalytic/thermoelectric tests across the temperature range.
frame.predicted_observations: For nanoparticles with enhanced lattice distortion, one would predict a delayed onset of phase segregation with maintained single-phase crystallinity as compared to the minimal distortion set. Elemental mapping (e.g., via EDX or atom probe tomography) and X-ray diffraction should reveal that homogeneity is retained longer (or up to higher temperatures) than in the baseline nanoparticles.
frame.conditions_for_prediction: The predictions should hold under controlled environmental conditions replicating catalytic and thermoelectric operation, ensuring that the only variable between sets is the degree of lattice distortion (or related mixing energetics), and the temperature is ramped within 473–1923 K.
frame.supporting_evidence: Evidence would include consistent XRD patterns showing single-phase structure up to higher temperatures in the distorted set, coupled with localized elemental mapping confirming chemical homogeneity, and kinetic measurements (e.g., diffusion coefficients) indicating slower atomic rearrangement.
frame.falsification_criteria: If both sets of nanoparticles exhibit similar onset and rates of phase segregation or chemical ordering at comparable temperatures (despite different lattice distortions), or if characterization techniques reveal that atomic diffusion rates are not significantly affected by the modified mixing enthalpy and lattice distortion, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

decision.trend: Early studies assumed that high configurational entropy and average electronic/thermodynamic descriptors alone would guarantee the persistent single‐phase state of multimetal nanoparticles. Researchers then moved on to examine phase transitions and catalytic performance under reactive conditions, which revealed that temperature‐activated atomic diffusion and local lattice distortions can induce segregation or chemical ordering despite high mixing entropy. Most recently, work on lattice distortion scaling laws has quantified how static size mismatches (and related mixing enthalpy differences) effectively shift the balance against temperature-driven diffusion, yet the precise interplay between these competing factors under catalytic/thermoelectric conditions remains understudied.
decision.unsolved: It remains unresolved how the competition between temperature-activated atomic diffusion and the stabilizing effects of lattice distortions (driven by atomic size mismatch and mixing enthalpy) dictates the maintenance of a homogeneous single-phase structure over the wide catalytic/thermoelectric operating range (473–1923 K).
decision.lever: Systematically substitute one element to increase lattice distortion (for example, replacing one constituent with an element exhibiting a larger atomic radius mismatch and higher mixing enthalpy penalty) while keeping the overall equimolar composition constant, then perform in-situ high-temperature XRD and elemental mapping across 473–1923 K.
decision.why: This step directly isolates the role of lattice distortion in resisting temperature-driven diffusion, building on trends that moved from entropy-based predictions to quantifying distortion effects; by controlling this lever, the experiment can test whether enhanced lattice distortions delay the onset of phase segregation and chemical ordering under realistic catalytic/thermoelectric conditions.
